In [22]:
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
stl = STL(endog,period=30)
result = stl.fit()
plt.figure(figsize =(14,10))
plt.subplot(411)
plt.plot(result.observed,label="Original",color="#FF914D")
plt.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.subplot(412)
plt.plot(result.trend,label="Trend",color="#FF914D")
plt.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.subplot(413)
plt.plot(result.seasonal,label="Seasonality",color="#FF914D")
plt.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.subplot(414)
plt.plot(result.resid,label="Residual",color="#FF914D")
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Stationarity

When,
(weak stationarity) mean(no trend)
variance
acf all remain constant

Makes prediction easier it assumes same statistical properties throughout time

Forecasting models require a stationary data

Strong stationarity means : Joint distribution will remain the same even when shifted across time

For different forecasting models and shorter periods of data--> weak stationarity
For long time of forecasting, we need stationarity strong to model entire data distribution

Test for stationarity

Weak stationarity
ADF test
and Kpss test

ADF test:presence of unit root which is a non stationary trend.
H0 Null hypothesis --> data has a unit root(non stationary)
H1 Alt Hypothesis -->stationary.
If significance value is 0.05, and p<0.05 we reject null hypothesis

Kpss Test Fits a constant mean model on the data and measures variance of the cumulative sum of residual,
H0 Null hypothesis --> stationary
H1 Alt Hypothesis -->non stationary
if p < significance value, we reject null hypothesis and data is non stationary

Strict stationarity Test: KS Test checks empirical/cumulative distribution functions of two samples.
if p>significance value there is no difference in distribution(stationary)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import kstest,ks_2samp
np.random.seed(0)
n = 500
#normal distribution random noise ---> strict stationary data
strict_stationary_series = np.random.normal(0,1,n)
#non strictly stationary--> introduce variance
non_strict_stationary_series = np.concatenate([np.random.normal(0,1,n//2),
np.random.normal(0,2,n//2)])
def ks_test_stationary(series):
    split = len(series)//2
    series_first_half = series[:split]
    series_second_half = series[split:]
    stat, p_value = ks_2samp(series_first_half, series_second_half)
    return stat,p_value
ks_stat_strict,ks_pvalue_strict = ks_test_stationary(strict_stationary_series)
ks_stat_nonstrict,ks_pvalue_nonstrict = ks_test_stationary(non_strict_stationary_series)
plt.figure(figsize=(14,6))
plt.subplot(411)

plt.plot(strict_stationary_series,label="Strict Stationary ks stat {ks_stat_strict} and pvalue {ks_pvalue_strict}",color="#FF914D")

plt.subplot(412)
plt.plot(non_strict_stationary_series,label="Non Strict Stationary ks stat {ks_stat_nonstrict} and pvalue {ks_pvalue_nonstrict}",color="#FF914D")
print(f"Strict Stationary ks stat {ks_stat_strict} and pvalue {ks_pvalue_strict}")
print(f"Non Strict Stationary ks stat {ks_stat_nonstrict} and pvalue {ks_pvalue_nonstrict}")

Non Strict Stationary ks stat 0.184 and pvalue 0.00040888636357191906

def weak_stationary_test(series):
    kpss_test = kpss(series,regression = "ct")
    print("Kpss Test Results")
    print(f"Kpss statistic: {round(kpss_test[0],3)}")
    print(f'p-value:{kpss_test[1]}')
    print('Critical Values:')
    for key, value in kpss_test[3].items():
        print(f'{key}: {value}')
    adf_test = adfuller(series)
    print("Adf Test Results")
    print(f"Adf statistic: {round(adf_test[0],3)}")
    print(f"p-value: {round(adf_test[1],3)}")
    print('Critical Values:')
    for key, value in adf_test[4].items():
        print(f'{key}: {round(value,3)}')
        
    if(kpss_test[1]<0.05 and round(adf_test[1],3)>0.05):
        return "Non stationary"
    elif(kpss_test[1]>0.05 and round(adf_test[1],3)<0.05):
        return "Stationary"
    else:
        return "can't conclude"

White Noise and Random Walk

White noise: if a time series data has no pattern, trend or seasonality. Same mean, constant variance and no acf , then it has white noise. very random-->unpredictable

Random Walk(non stationary) : cumulative pattern yt = yt-1 +e , it is predictable. Mean and variance change overtime. First diff is stationary then it becomes predictable

Check how: Visual analysis ACF and PACF Ljung Box

In [42]:
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
np.random.seed(0)
n = 1000
#Generate white noise
np.random.normal(0,1,n)
white_noise = np.random.normal(0,1,n)
#randomwalk generate
random_shocks = np.random.normal(0,1,n)
random_walk = np.cumsum(random_shocks)

plt.figure(figsize=(14,6))
plt.subplot(2,1,1)
plt.plot(white_noise,color = "#FF194D")
plt.title(f"White Noise")


plt.subplot(2,1,2)
plt.plot(random_walk,color="#FF194D")
plt.title(f"Random Walk")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

#Ljung-Box test

print('\nLjung Box Test for white noise')
lb_test_white_noise = acorr_ljungbox(white_noise, lags = [10], return_df = True)
print(lb_test_white_noise)

Ljung Box Test for white noise
     lb_stat  lb_pvalue
10  8.297906   0.599763

Since Lb_pvalue>0.05 for white noise,

H0:white noise
H1:not white noise
H0:random walk
H1:not random walk
if p<0.05 we know it is reject null hypothesis, it is random walk

Since here lb_pvalue>0.05 we can't reject null hypothesis, it is white noise
Since here random walk lbpvalue<0.05 we reject the null hypothesis it is not random_walk

from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
import numpy as np
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
#Fit the auto regressive model to the training data
model = AutoReg(train_data, lags = 30)
model_fit = model.fit()
# Using integer indices based on array length
start_idx = len(train_data)
end_idx = len(train_data) + len(test_data) - 1
prediction = model_fit.predict(start=start_idx, end=end_idx, dynamic=False)   
#Plot the actual vs predicted values

#plot the actual vs predicted values
plt.figure(figsize =(10,5))
plt.plot(test_data.index, test_data, label="Test data")
plt.plot(test_data.index,prediction,color='red',linestyle="--",label ="Predicted Prices")
plt.title("Apple Stock Prices : Actual vs predicted")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel('Close Price')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

rmse = round(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test_data, prediction)),2)

print(f"RMSE:{rmse}")

We performed bilateral testing. We have tested if apple stocks get affected by tesla, or if it is vice versa, or both.

























h0 : x does not granger cause y

h1 : x granger causes y

Here we see in case 1, where AAPL is dependent y and Tesla is independent x,  p value comes out to be ~ 0 < 0.05 so we reject the null hypothesis, apple stock prices at close are dependent on tesla stock prices at close.

In case 2 we see, the p value > 0.05 , so null hypothesis can't be rejected, so we can say apple stock closing prices donot granger cause tesla stock closing prices.

from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR, VARMAX
import pandas as pd
#VAR
model = VAR(train_data)
result = model.fit(maxlags = 7)
predictions = result.forecast(train_data.values[-result.k_ar:],steps = len(test_data))

plt.figure(figsize =(10,6))

plt.plot(test_data.index, predictions['TSLA_Close'],label = "Predicted Price",color = "red")

plt.title('Tesla Stock Prediction')

weighted moving average
exponential smoothing























Exponential smoothing: time series with no trend or seasonality 
 Holt's model : for trend
Winter Model: trend and seasonality



















In [37]:



     


window_size = 20
stock_data["SMA"] = stock_data["Close"].rolling(window = window_size).mean()

weights = np.arange(1,window_size+1)
stock_data["WMA"] = stock_data['Close'].rolling(window_size).apply(lambda prices:np.dot(prices,weights)/weights.sum(),raw=True)
stock_data['EMA'] = stock_data['Close'].ewm(span = window_size).mean()

plt.figure(figsize =(10,6))
plt.plot(stock_data['Close'],label = 'Close Price',color ='blue',alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot(stock_data['SMA'],label = f'SMA {window_size}-day',color ='green')
plt.plot(stock_data['WMA'],label = f'WMA {window_size}-day',color ='orange')
plt.plot(stock_data['EMA'],label = f'EMA {window_size}-day',color ='red')

plt.title('Apple Stock Price with SMA, WMA and, EMA')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.ylabel('Price (USD)')
plt.legend()
plt.grid()
plt.show()

#Simple exponential, Holt's and Winter's model



     



















In [41]:



     


from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import SimpleExpSmoothing, ExponentialSmoothing

close_prices = stock_data['Close']

ses_model = SimpleExpSmoothing(close_prices,initialization_method="estimated").fit(smoothing_level = 0.7)
stock_data['SES'] = ses_model.fittedvalues

des_model = ExponentialSmoothing(close_prices, trend = 'add'). fit(smoothing_level=0.7)
stock_data['DES'] = des_model.fittedvalues

tes_model = ExponentialSmoothing(close_prices, trend = 'add',seasonal = 'add', seasonal_periods = 12). fit(smoothing_level=0.7)
stock_data['TES'] = tes_model.fittedvalues



plt.figure(figsize =(10,6))
plt.plot(stock_data['Close'],label = 'Close Price',color ='blue',alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot(stock_data['SES'],label = 'Single exponential smoothing',color ='green')
plt.plot(stock_data['DES'],label = 'Holt Model',color ='yellow')
plt.plot(stock_data['TES'],label = 'Winter Model',color ='red')

plt.title('Apple Stock Price with SES, DES and, TES')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.ylabel('Price (USD)')
plt.legend()
plt.grid()
plt.show()

Auto correlation and Partial Auto correlation function























Correlation between x and lagged version of x























For stationary data: ACF decays exponentially or sinosoidally

Model         ACF                          PACF

AR            Tails off, decays     cuts off after lag p

MA            cuts off after q     tails off  

ARMA(if non stationary arima)        tails off              tails off























ACF gives q value
PACF gives p value



















In [51]:



     


from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf , plot_pacf
plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))
#acf
plt.subplot(1,2,1)
plot_acf(stock_data['Close'].diff().dropna(),ax=plt.gca(),lags = 50)
plt.title("ACF")
#pacf
plt.subplot(1,2,2)
plot_pacf(stock_data['Close'].diff().dropna(),ax=plt.gca(),lags = 50,method='ywm')
plt.title("PACF")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

In [67]:



     


from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
apple_price_stationary = stock_data["Close"]
train_data, test_data = apple_price_stationary[:-30], apple_price_stationary[-30:]
train_data = train_data.reset_index(drop=True)
test_data = test_data.reset_index(drop=True)   

model = AutoReg(train_data, lags = 30)
model_fit = model.fit()
# Using integer indices based on array length
start_idx = len(train_data)
end_idx = len(train_data) + len(test_data) - 1
prediction = model_fit.predict(start=start_idx, end=end_idx, dynamic=False)   
#Plot the actual vs predicted values

#plot the actual vs predicted values
plt.figure(figsize =(10,5))
plt.plot(test_data.index, test_data, label="Test data")
plt.plot(test_data.index,prediction,color='red',linestyle="--",label ="Predicted Prices")
plt.title("Apple Stock Prices : Actual vs predicted")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel('Close Price')
plt.legend()
plt.show()
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
rmse = round(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test_data, prediction)),2)
mae = round(mean_absolute_error(test_data,prediction),2)
mape = np.mean(np.abs((list(test_data.to_numpy().flatten())-prediction.to_numpy().flatten())/list(test_data.to_numpy().flatten())))*100
print(f"RMSE:{rmse}")
print(f"MAE:{mae}")
print(f"RMSE:{rmse**2}")
print(f"MAPE:{mape}")
print(f"AIC:{model_fit.aic}")
print(f"AIC:{model_fit.bic}")
